utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to sit down and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good morning, Dr. Treanor. Can you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: My name is Patrick Joseph Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would like to call up 65 ter 14044, initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Treanor, is this a copy of your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And having had an opportunity to look at it, does it need any quick updating?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is a few years old. I have retired since this resume was produced. I retired from ICTY and the UN at the end of 2009. I think this resume also does not reflect the fact that I did testify as an expert in the Perisic case and that I have submitted expert reports in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 14044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2536, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, bearing in mind that the court now has your CV in evidence, I would ask if you could very quickly provide a synopsis of your experience as it relates to the three reports that you prepared in the context of this case. Those would be 65 ter 00592, the Bosnian Serb leadership, 1990 through 1992; 65 ter 12124, the Bosnian Serb leadership, 1993 through 1995; and 65 ter 1215, Radovan Karadzic and the Serbian leadership, 1990 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, these reports represent in a certain respect the totality -- the product of the totality of my training and experience in this area. I began studying Slavic languages when I was in college. I began studying the languages and history and culture of the Balkan countries, including Yugoslavia, during my study for a Masters Degree which I received in 1970. I continued studying that area in Bulgaria for two years in the 1970s and went to the University of London and began a Ph.D. in the mid-1970s. I began professionally working in this area in 1977 when I started to work as an intelligence analyst at the US Library of Congress reading -- reading the press and technical including military journals from the Soviet Union and eastern Europe including the former Yugoslavia. A few years later I began working at the U.S. Department of Justice investigating the cases of alleged Nazi war criminals living in or seeking entry into the United States. I had a wide area of responsibilities there, including the former Yugoslavia. During the course of that work I did research in numerous countries, archives in numerous countries, including the former Yugoslavia, Belgrade, Zagreb, Sarajevo, and Banja Luka. I then came to this institution in 1994, when -- when I began almost immediately doing research on the Bosnian Serb leadership and have been concentrating substantively in that area during the whole period of my time with the Tribunal in addition, of course, to my later supervisory and other responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, it's quickly clear from these reports that a large number of documents are cited, described, and used in the context of the reports. Were you involved in the collection of documents that were used in -- in your reports?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The focusing on my work here again these reports represent the product of the result of 15 years of work here which began in 1994 when I began the effort with other people to identify and collect the highest level and other documents produced by the Serbian Democratic Party and Bosnia and the various governmental organs of Republika Srpska. As I said, we began that effort in 1994, and I pursued a methodical effort to obtain the most important documentation, certainly including Official Gazettes, press from the area, and the records from the highest level government and state bodies including minutes of meetings, reports, decisions, orders, correspondence, diaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. And when you say methodical just a couple of quick questions on that. Did you attempt to obtain entire collections of documents, selected collections, and secondly, did you attempt to collect documents during the course of your work related to all parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, let me take the first -- the second part of that question first. Yes, as the leader of the leadership research team, we were involved in collecting documents and doing research and analysis on all the parties to the conflicts. My -- most of my personal work, personal substantive work continued to involve the Bosnian Serbs. I'm sorry, what was the first part of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Whether or not the collection of documents was aimed at the entirety of collections that you could obtain related to those types of documents --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- if there was any other process.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: We sought to obtain access to the totality of the documentation, the records, the archives of whatever particular institution was the purpose of a given mission, for instance, whether it be the Presidency, the Ministry of Internal Affairs, Ministry of Defence, et cetera. Depending on the situation, we would either have to review those documents in situ and make a selection of documents and have them copied and bring them back to The Hague, or sometimes we were in a position to, in fact, get a copy, have the whole copy -- the whole collection scanned in situ or in one case we had the entire archive physically transferred to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, while it's fresh in my memory, there are a number of documents the Prosecution's informed the Chamber that it wishes to use with Dr. Treanor. Some it was proposed to be bar table, but you will recall that if you wish to tender those documents evidence of the truth of the contents, the Chamber's preferred method of admission is through the witness rather than by bar table motion. So any documents that you wish to use are best adduced through this witness in his evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Understood the priorities, Your Honour, which is in part why there's a judicious selection of bar table documents. On the other hand, in an effort to assist the Chamber to the greatest degree possible, we've tried to contextualise as much of the documentation that we may at this time or at a later time submit by way of bar table. So it's of as much assistance to the Chamber as possible. So trying to balance those -- all those factors, but I understood the Court's priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, can you tell the Court what criteria you employed in selecting the documents that you used in your report or relied upon in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to the reports themselves, you have to bear in mind that by the time the reports were written we had collected a huge volume of documentation. And in approaching selection of documents for the reports themselves, I used my knowledge of those collections and my expert knowledge of the area in general in -- in approaching the -- the topics of the reports which were requested in broad terms. I decided what had topics that I would deal with in those reports, and I selected documents that I thought would best convey the story of the chronological progress of those various topics. I -- in doing so, I sought to use, as I think I've emphasised in the introduction to the reports, the most authoritative documents; that is, documents from the highest level state and party organs. Sometimes -- and again that would be such things as records of meetings, decisions, orders, correspondence, items from Official Gazettes. Absent such things sometimes I've used other less authoritative documents, perhaps such as items from the press. I tried to confine myself in that case to items that actually reflected the words of various leaders rather than simple journalistic reports or opinion pieces and that type of thing. So the reports are based on the -- for the most part on the actual documentation of the Bosnian Serb leaders themselves. When it comes to the negotiations reports are used produced by the international negotiators who were also obviously participants in those particular events and in various discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, there are, as I mentioned earlier, clearly a large number of documents and I think you referred to entire collections. Did -- were you assisted in identifying the documents that were potentially relevant to the issues addressed in your report by other members of LRT, and if so, that is other members of the leadership research team, and if so, what control did you exercise over the material that was eventually relied upon in your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Initially I did all the -- all the collection and all the analysis and indeed some of the early writing myself. The team wasn't established until 1997. At that point when addition -- I began to bring additional people on board. I assigned people to work in particular areas in this case in relation to the Bosnian Serbs, to work on areas such as the SDS or the Presidency, and they were responsible for analysing documents in those areas, producing analysis of them, all of which they did under my supervision and all of which work I reviewed, and indeed I've read virtually all the documents themselves in addition. And therefore especially for the first report, sections -- the initial sections of that report were -- were drafted by other people, but again I reviewed the entire report on the basis of my knowledge of the documents and therefore take full responsibility for that report. I think in the addendum and the leadership study it is explicitly stated that other people were involved. The involvement at that point related to mostly the -- the use of CaseMap, which we started using in this institution I think around the time that the first report, the main report was produced in 2002, whatever it was, and it was our practice to -- it was my practice to put notes, summaries or extracts or sometimes entire document of the various bodies that I've been referring to into our -- into our team CaseMap, and I assigned people to that task to work on particular sets of documents, et cetera, and I reviewed all that work extensively and on an ongoing basis and made sure that the work was as complete as possible and the addendum to the report and the leadership study were largely produced out -- directly -- not directly but produced out of the CaseMap in which I and other people on my team, including interns, worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so when you say in your report that you bear sole responsibility for the contents, what do you mean by that, Dr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: By that I mean that I have -- as I said, I have familiarity with all the documents, have read virtually all of them myself, and have either wrote myself or very closely edited and checked anything that was written by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 00592, 12124, and 12125 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I assign the numbers to the three expert reports, there's a small correction. The CV 65 ter number 14044 was assigned Exhibit P2536. In fact, it will be Exhibit P2535. And then 65 ter number 592 will be Exhibit number P2536, 65 ter number 12124 will be Exhibit P2537, and 65 ter number 12125 will be Exhibit P2538.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, I'd ask you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd ask the registrar to call up 65 ter 00932. This is an interview with Dr. Karadzic that appeared in a publication "Nin" in November of 1990, and before I ask you about that, if I could ask you to very briefly, and again bearing in mind that your reports are now in front of the Court, place the -- this interview in context.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. I'd just briefly remind the report that this interview in "Nin" which is a Belgrade weekly news magazine came out about a week before the -- a week or ten days before the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which took place on the 18th of November, 1990. In the months preceding that election, a number of political parties had been founded in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Serbian Democratic Party which was founded on the 12th of July, 1990, at an Assembly in Sarajevo which elected Radovan Karadzic the president of the party and adopted a programme and a statute. The statute outlined the organisation and operations of the party, created an organisational structure that -- a hierarchical structure that more or less paralleled the governmental structure of -- of the Republic of BH going from the central level in the party which included the president, a Main Board, which is a policy-making party -- body between Assemblies. The Assembly which would meet every year or so, an executive body to handle business matters, and going down to having regional boards. There was no regional level of government in Bosnia, but they did have regional co-ordinating party bodies to co-ordinate the Municipal Boards which were very important. Municipality was the fundamental governmental institution on the local level in the republic. So the -- every party Municipal Boards were very important, and then below that there were even local community boards, the municipalities being composed of what they called local communities. And they had organised by this time throughout almost the entire country and almost every municipality in the country the party had managed to establish some sort of organisation and the -- just briefly mentioning the programme of the party included a variety of points which are -- would be rather typical for a political party, social and economic issues, but the point that deserves emphasis here is the desire, the expressed desire of the -- expressed in the programme and at Dr. Karadzic's speech to the Assembly, the desire of the Bosnian Serbs to remain in Yugoslavia in one state with the other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of quick follow-up questions with respect the hierarchical structure of the SDS. First, was there any effort or emphasis placed on the importance of that hierarchy in respect to the flow of information or instructions from the top level to the bottom level?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, in the statute of the party, it was specified that all party members were obliged to adhere to the policy of the party, and the party developed over time a very efficient system of communications within the party to convey instructions down from the top and to receive reports up from the bottom. Or I should say it attempted to create an efficient system. I think in this article we'll see how successful they've been to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from 1990 to 1995, who was at the top of that hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, at the top of the hierarchy was Dr. Karadzic as president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention first to paragraph 4 of page 1 of this article. There's -- there's reference to the revival of the political life of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and to organisational work which had been completed in a very short time, and then we see a reference to the local boards and "each member of a local board of the Serbian Democratic Party is in contact with 10 to 20 Serbian households so that information from the most remote village reaches the Main Board in two hours at most."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, this is an indication of how successful their organisational efforts had been, and this ability to communicate down to that level, in fact, get in contact with all Serbian households was particularly important immediately at this time a connection with the campaign of -- in connection with the upcoming elections. They used this ability to transmit campaign literature and instructions, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 6 of the English and it would be the next page, I believe, in B/C/S. At the bottom of the page we see the reference "Everybody knows that under no circumstances will Serbs accept to live in several independent states and to become a national minority everywhere outside Serbia. The Serbs will stay in one state, federal Yugoslavia, regardless of its size." And if we could look quickly at the last page, page 8, the last paragraph of the article or interview. " We -- we are now openly saying," Dr. Karadzic states here, "what could not even be whispered before. The Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina pin all their hopes on their mother country Serbia and will never allow a state border to separate them from Serbia." If you could place that in the -- in context both in terms of what you spoke about before.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, here is Dr. Karadzic forcefully stating the point in the programme related to the desire of the Bosnian Serbs to remain in one state with the other Serbs, which was a very, very important part of their message in -- during the election campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally if we could turn to page 3 of the English, third paragraph from the bottom which states that: "Serbs could be out-voted by a two-thirds majority regarding, for instance, the issues of the change of the state character of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Should that happen, all conditions for a civil war would be in place because the Serbs in BH are no longer helpless but very powerful and united."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Here Dr. Karadzic is referring to the main concern that they had in connection with their remaining in Yugoslavia, that is that the other -- members of the other peoples, the other nations in Bosnia, may want to split from Yugoslavia. The Serbs had a very large minority, about a third of the population, but not a majority. So -- so that they were concerned that the other people may simply out-vote them and take Bosnia out of Yugoslavia, which they saw as highly detrimental to their interests. They therefore at around this time, that is October, November 1990, took some steps to try to prevent that. For one thing, Dr. Karadzic had -- sent a letter to the existing BH Assembly asking that a Chamber of nationalities be established which would be able to block any measures that individual peoples saw as going against their interests. That didn't draw any response, and they found -- also found that at this time a Serbian National Council in Bosnia which proclaimed, as mentioned in the report, proclaimed itself to be the sole representative of the Serbian nation in Bosnia and saying that they would not accept any decisions by the Assembly or anyone else that ran counter to the interests of the -- the Serbian people in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 00932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2539, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, the article -- or the interview -- or in the course of the interview we have just looked at a passage where Dr. Karadzic states that in the event of being out-voted on the issue of the change of state character, all conditions for a civil war would be in place. Did that situation arise and did Dr. Karadzic indicate what that war would be like?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. That situation did arise, and he did indicate what -- what such a war might be like on a number of occasions. That situation arose in the middle of October 1991, that is about a year later after a long back and forth which I didn't go into. The -- basically the Muslim and Croatian deputies in the new BH Assembly, that is the Assembly that was created as a result of the 1990 elections, did in fact vote resolutions which the Bosnian Serbs, known as the referendum and the letter for short, which they're mentioned in my reports, which the Bosnian Serbs regarded as being basically declarations of independence of Bosnia. These resolutions were passed in the absence of those -- of the -- of the SDS deputies to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and they regarded them as being illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I call up 30351, please. This is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic, Miodrag Davidovic, and Luka Karadzic on the 15th of October, 1991. And if I could ask the registrar to call up page 5 of both the English and the B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking at the bottom of the page in English, Dr. Karadzic states: "They want an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is an attempt to create it. Is this hell, man? Twelve percent of Serbs made hell in Croatia, they didn't allow a Ustasha state to be introduced into their homes, and these here are trying to with 35 per cent, you know." Turn to the next page in English, please. And there Dr. Karadzic continues after a brief exchange: "Who -- what are you talking about? Who'll do it man? That would mean war until their extinction. The Serbs would never forgive them such a thing. It would destroy them completely. First none of their leaders would survive. They'd all be killed in three to four hours. They'd stand no chance of surviving whatsoever." Dr. Treanor, can you place this conversation in context for us, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This conversation which takes place between Dr. Karadzic and his brother and a family friend in Montenegro took place later in the day after the resolutions regarding the sovereignty of BH were passed. Those resolution were is passed very early in the morning of the 15th of October, and this is obviously taking place after that, and he's commenting on his view of what that means and what the -- what the result could be, namely war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender 30351, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, would ask that that be received as marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P2540.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor in -- earlier you mentioned and mentioned it again here the concern about out-voting. Let me ask you if more generally the SDS and Dr. Karadzic were concerned about the ethnic structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were concerned with the changes that were taking place in the ethnic structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at a couple of documents. First, 18625, page 24 of the B/C/S and page 28 of the English, in particular. And, Dr. Treanor, can you place this in the context of your earlier response, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Dr. Karadzic in his speech to the founding Assembly of the SDS had noted among other things the exodus of tens if not hundreds of thousands of Serbs from BH over the previous decades, and that was a situation that -- which among others was of great concern to him and the other SDS leaders. They had a number of studies on the demographic changes taking place in Bosnia prepared. This particular study was done by Milorad Skoko, who was the SDS appointee as the deputy director of the republic institute of social planning. This -- this report was -- is dated June 1991. He later updated that report. This graph has -- the same graph has appeared in at least one of his later reports and other people wrote similar reports. The thing that I want to point out here about the graph, as you can see the top two lines relate to the growth of the Muslim population in -- in two different variants, both of which show that population increasing sharply; whereas, the next line down, rather flat, is the Serbs, and below that is the Croatian -- the Croats, which is also rather flat. They, they being the SDS leaders, therefore feared that for instance in an independent BH the Muslims would soon gain an absolute majority in that republic and therefore would be able to run the republic any way they saw fit and without any regard to the concerns of the other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, tender page 24 of the B/C/S, page 28 of the English this chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2541, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to 000 -- excuse me 06639. And to page 12 of the English and the page marked SA043638 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Dr. Treanor, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: This is a notebook kept by Vojislav Maksimovic who was an SDS deputy in the BH Assembly and was, in fact, the president of their deputy's club or caucus in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if -- we're now looking at an entry for a meeting of the political council on 24th of December, 1991, and turning your attention to the remarks of Professor Najdanovic who asks: "What are our maximum number borders? We need a single Serbian state which cannot be inhabited by Muslims because they would overwhelm us with their birth rate." Can you first tell us who Professor Najdanovic was, what the political council was, and place the -- his comments in context?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, first all the political council was an advisory body established by the SDS which included non-party intellectuals as well as party people. It was a forum for -- a regular forum for discussion. I think they tried to meet every week or so. Dr. Karadzic attended frequently. This body provided the SDS leadership with input on a variety of issues that they tried to get the best possible expert advice on the issues of the day. Professor Slavko Leovac is mentioned, who appears right at the top of that entry, was the president of the council. Professor Milutin Najdanovic was an SDS deputy in the Assembly. He was also a deputy in the Federal Assembly in Belgrade, a member of the chamber of republics. Now, this meeting took place on the 24th of December, 1991. We're moving along now in time. This is just a few days after the Presidency and the government of BH formally requested international recognition of the independence of BH from various other states and international bodies. This, of course, was something that the Bosnian Serbs were also bitterly opposed to. It was a logical step, indeed, from the October 15th resolutions. So at this time they were, they being the Bosnian Serb leaders, were contemplating as an alternative to trying to keep the whole of BH within Yugoslavia and all the Serbs in it. As an alternative to that, defining a -- Serbian territories within BH which could in some manner be separated from BH in order that those territories remain in Yugoslavia; whereas, the Croats and Muslim, if they so chose, would be free to leave Yugoslavia. So professor Najdanovic is contemplating what such a state might look like ethnographically and is stating that it couldn't have too many Muslims in it because even if they were a minority at the beginning with their birth rate they would soon become a majority and then we wouldn't have a Serbian state any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And does that concern recur during the course of discussions about the ethnic structure of a Serbian BH or other aspects of a policy during the years 1991 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, you see this type of comment several times in various sessions of the Assembly over the course of years, and immediately after this -- not immediately, but a month after this the new Bosnian Serb Council of Ministers in fact requested an update of that demographic report that we saw earlier. So this was an issue that was -- was very much in their minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd tender 06639, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Mr. President. I'd like to make an objection to that. I think that this is of no probative value, what somebody says in a meeting. For example, would Tony Blair be charged with something that somebody said in the house of commons, or would President Obama be responsible for what somebody of the Tea Party says in Congress? So I don't think there's any probative value to statements made by somebody in some body unless it's adopted by Dr. Karadzic or in some way attributed to him. I would ask that this exhibit be excluded as having no probative value. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would not like this to count against my time. First of all, this is one piece of evidence in the totality of evidence which the Court has already received and will be receiving with respect to this issue, which is one of the reasons I asked Dr. Treanor if this issue recurs in other fora at other times and consistently. And it's a false argument to say that one piece of evidence standing alone has a limited weight when it's clearly part of the mosaic of evidence that will be relied upon and can be relied upon by the Court to know what issues underpin Bosnian Serb policy. Furthermore, the witness indicated the relationship between this speaker as a member of the political council and Dr. Karadzic, and I can elucidate that, but I think it's clear in his -- he made clear in his report, made clear in his answer that these are people upon whom Dr. Karadzic relies and turns to for information and opinion and views upon which to frame policy. I think this is a specious objection, and clearly this document should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The Bench is unanimous on this. If this was a piece of evidence that stood alone, then its probative value would be assessed, if any, on that basis, but it's part of a mosaic. Again, that doesn't require or suggest that it has a specific probative value at this stage, but it has the potential for having a probative value and without it the jigsaw is not as complete, and on that basis it will at this stage be admitted for consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2542, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you referred to the importance of the position by the Bosnian Serb leadership regarding not allowing a border to separate Serbs from other Serbs, for example, in Serbia. I'd like to call up 06583. First I want to ask you if that fundamental aspiration to which you referred of keeping the Serbs united ever changed during the course of the period 1990 through 1995.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: No. It never -- it never changed. If I may be allowed to elucidate on my previous answer perhaps I was not as helpful to the Court as I could have been. Dr. Karadzic himself did make comments on -- on more than one occasion reflecting the type of demographic concerns that we saw expressed in that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the tactical approach for achieving that objective change over time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. The tactics did change.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And looking quickly at 06583, and in particular the bottom of the page, this is a -- these are the minutes of a session of the club of deputies held on 30 September 1991, and at the bottom we see reflected a comment by Dr. Karadzic: "The war goal of the Serbian people is Yugoslavia for the simple reason that it is much harder to tear something apart than to hold onto the old legality." If you could place that in context, please, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this comment was made at a meeting of the -- of the deputy -- SDS deputy's club which I referred to. Dr. Karadzic was not a deputy but as the party leader he did attend their meetings. At this point in September 1991, as discussed in my -- I think in the report and in the leadership study, negotiations were going on between the Bosnian Serb leaders and leaders of the other national communities about the future of Bosnia. One of the overriding goal, as Dr. Karadzic puts it here, for them -- for the Bosnian Serbs is to remain in Bosnia. I note the war goal is put in quotation marks. I think he means that in the sense of their overriding goal, their chief priority. Their -- their strategy at this point was to a large extent based on the fact that Bosnia was a part of Yugoslavia and it would remain so until a decision was taken to take it out. He thought that at this point that he had agreement as reflected a little bit up the page there, Mr. Izetbegovic's agreement that one people would not attempt to impose their will on another; that is, anything that would happen would happen by consensus. So resting on the legal status quo, which was perfectly acceptable to the Bosnian Serbs, that is they were in Yugoslavia, they thought they had the easy part. All they had to do was maintain the status quo. So that was the basis of their approach at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 06583.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could look next at P00938 [Realtime transcript read in error "P00958"], page 37 of the English and page 55 of the B/C/S. It's 938. The transcript says "958." So I don't know if there's confusion for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Looking at the middle of the page in English. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking as we can see from the earlier portion of the transcript, and he states: "Please, until two or three months ago we were hoping to be able to play the Yugoslav card and say the Yugoslav army, Yugoslavia legality, et cetera, this is slipping out of our grasp. That's why we started on another track, the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, our sovereign right, our army." You've alluded to that before. If you could place that quickly in the context of your earlier remarks.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. These remarks were made at the meeting of the SDS deputies club at the end of February 1991, during a time when very intensive negotiations were taking place under international auspices among the leaders of the national communities in Bosnia as to the future of Bosnia. This comment reflects the fact that the Bosnian Serb leaders, Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders, the SDS leaders. Had -- had to change their strategy. He makes reference to two or three months ago. That was about December 1991. Without going into too much detail, because I think it is discussed in the -- certainly in the leadership study, that was the time when the war in Croatia which involved the Croatian Serbs, who had similar concerns about remaining in Croatia to those of the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia, that war was drawing to an end. An agreement was being put, formulated by Mr. Cyrus Vance, ultimately known as the Vance Plan, to bring a measure of peace to that republic. The Croatian Serbs also wanted to stay within Yugoslavia. However, the leadership in Belgrade made it clear at meetings in Belgrade in December 1991, that Dr. Karadzic attended, that Serbia could not continue the war. It did not have the strength, and they were going to -- the best thing at that time was for the Croatian Serbs to -- was to accept the -- the recognition they were getting from the international community of the existence of their territories, and that after some intermediate period under UN supervision they were assured by the Belgrade leadership that they would then get to join Yugoslavia or Serbia or whatever Serbian state may exist. The same held good for Bosnia. Again, it -- basically for international reasons and the reasons of exhaustion of Serbia, it was not going to be as simple as staying in Yugoslavia. The international community would have regarded that as aggression on the part of Serbia against Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore the leadership in Belgrade decided that they had to go ahead and form a new FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, consisting of just Serbia and Montenegro and not any other areas -- Serbian areas -- Serbian claimed areas outside those two republics. They did ultimately in the constitution of that, the new FRY in April 1992, leave the door over to accession by other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the time these remarks we just looked at were made, with respect to the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina referred to by Dr. Karadzic, were efforts underway to define its -- to establish its structures, define its territorial scope and so on at that point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Serbs were making their own efforts to do that, and the basis of the negotiations at that time was the formation and the recognition of separate entities within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before either the establishment of a Bosnian Serb -- well, before the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Republic or before the specific efforts taking place at this time, that is in late February 1992 were underway, had there been efforts to identify or earmark territories within Bosnia and Herzegovina considered to be Serbia by the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when such efforts had -- had begun?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the efforts that I would refer to go under the generic name of regionalisation. Regionalisation did not figure by name in the programme of the SDS, but Dr. Karadzic did speak about it very shortly after the first Assembly meeting in July 1990. He did speak about regionalisation. The Serbs -- the Bosnian Serbs were dissatisfied with the way municipal boundaries had been drawn in BH to the detriment of the Serbs. They hoped to change those boundaries, and they also wanted to create regions of municipalities, that is group municipalities together by region to promote their interests, and they wanted to do this, form these regions, on basically an ethnic basis; that is, group Serbian majority municipalities together in their own regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Treanor, bearing in mind that P2536, your report entitled: "The Bosnian Serb Leadership 1990 through 1992," details in part 2 aspects related to regionalisation. Can I just ask you quickly to identify broadly the steps of regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Right. This effort actually got underway, started being discussed, as far as we know, as early as January 1991, that is, immediately after the elections being discussed in SDS circles. The first Serbian-dominated communities of municipalities were formed in April 1991. Community municipalities was a type of co-operative association that was recognised in the BH constitution. It was not a governmental structure per se but just a co-operative association of municipalities. But two -- at least two communities of municipalities were formed at that time, one in Herzegovina, the other in Bosnian Krajina by SDS-dominated municipalities, and later in September they -- they proceeded further with that development in the -- with the creation of so-called Serbian autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I ask you to look at a September document, then, 65 ter 10825.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, this is Exhibit P2530, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does this document refer to a decision related to regionalisation and autonomous regions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this particular document is a decision on appointing of the staff for regional organisation on September 25, 1991, and in paragraph 2 of the document is -- it refers to implementation of the decision and conclusions adopted at the Pale symposium of municipal, regional, and republic SDS organs of 7 September 1991.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This document is particularly important because it is one of the very few documents that we have that directly relate to the symposium and the decisions it took. From this document we know at least the names of the decisions. We doesn't have the -- I haven't been able to locate the texts of those decisions, but as the Court can see, they relate to the promulgation, as the translation says, of autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were there discussions about or references to the September 7th meeting either before or after in the documentary record?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. We have one or more intercepted telephone conversations which refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can I call up -- first of all -- like I said, document's been given -- the previous document's been given a P number and is admitted, I take it. The document I identified as 1 -- 10825. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's P2530 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn next to 65 ter 30194. In particular to page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic, and in this section Dr. Karadzic states: "I'm having a big Plenary meeting here tomorrow at 4.00, all my officials." Then he goes on to say "I've been to Trebinje and sacked some fools. I was there for nine hours." Can you place this in context of the September 7th meeting, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, based on internal evidence in the -- in the conversation, as I think laid out in a footnote in the report, I believe that this conversation in fact took place on the 6th of September, and here Dr. Karadzic is referring to a meeting -- a big meeting tomorrow, which would be the 7th. So I infer that he's referring to the meeting which is explicitly referenced in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to quickly turn to a conversation of September 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'd ask that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2544, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then turning next to 65 ter 30204. And that would be page 1 of both the English and B/C/S. This is a conversation between Mirko Jovic and Jovan Tintor. And on the first page Tintor states: "You know what, we have no -- we have no specifics. There will be chaos tomorrow. We passed -- we passed a decision yesterday that Bosnia can remain officially, but we'll split it into Serbian Bosnia, Croat Bosnia, and Muslim Bosnia." And in terms of the September 7th meeting, can you place this conversation in context, both the -- and explain what's -- what's being discussed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is a conversation between two lower-level SDS officials, one of whom, Jovan Tintor, was obviously -- or I would conclude was at the meeting, because he refers to the decision in the terms he uses here, that is, dividing Bosnia into a Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian Bosnia. That was the -- the thing I would comment on there, because it, I think, can be a little confusing. I know it confused me. The Bosnian Serbs wanted to have their own region regardless of whether -- or regions, regardless of whether Bosnia as a whole remained in federal Yugoslavia or not, and the basis of the negotiations that they were carrying on with the -- with Muslim leaders at this time, as set out in my report, certainly in the leadership study, was that there would be regionalisation in Bosnia, and this -- this was something that the Muslims were not particularly enthusiastic about to say the least. However, at the September 30th meeting that we saw a little bit previously, Dr. Karadzic was -- seemed to be very happy to announce that Izetbegovic was willing to discuss regionalisation. So this is the way regionalisation presented itself to -- to the Bosnian Serbs, that is, dividing Bosnia into a Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian Bosnia regardless of whether it stayed in Yugoslavia or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 30204, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: For identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2545, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you mentioned that in connection with the shift from the Yugo card or Yugo strategy as it's been mentioned to one of a Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, that efforts were made to define the scope of its territory and establish structures. What was the first institution of what was to be the Bosnian Serb Republic created, and what was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the first central institution that was created was the -- they called it the Bosnian -- the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH. That was established on the 24th of October, 1991, a few days after the adoption of the sovereignty resolutions I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can we call up 30379, please. And I'd like to look quickly at three passages there, the first one at page 1. This is a conversation held on the 24th of October, 1991, between Dr. Karadzic and Slobodan Milosevic. And at page 1 Dr. Karadzic says: "We have to -- to prepare everything, and we have prepared everything to create a de facto situation that cannot be -- which they will break their teeth on. They simply have to break them. There is no way we will live in a country with them. There's no way at all. That's it." And then if we could turn to page 7 of the English. That's the bottom of page 5 in B/C/S. Dr. Karadzic continues: "You tell him that the Serbs are moving on that you can't -- that you can't exert influence over us to mellow things down. We are moving on. We will establish full authority over the Serbian territories in BiH and none of his lawyers will be able to show his nose there. He will not be able to exercise power. He will not have control over 65 per cent of his territory. That is our goal." And then continuing on the bottom of the page: "Our steps are calculated and we have to establish authority and control over our territories so that he doesn't get a sovereign Bosnia. Croatia doesn't have control over 30 per cent of its territory, and Bosnia will not have control over 60 per cent of its territory." And can you place that in appropriate context for us, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Certainly. This conversation took place on the day that the Bosnian Serb Assembly was founded. However, it took place before the meeting at which that occurred. Dr. Karadzic had been in Belgrade the day before for a meeting of -- of Serbian leaders. Whether he spoke to Mr. Milosevic directly at that time, I don't know. Mr. Milosevic, in this conversation, is trying to, in fact, dissuade Dr. Karadzic from taking the step of founding an Assembly, saying you shouldn't answer one illegal step, that is the proclamation of Bosnian sovereignty, with another illegal step, that is the formation of this Assembly. But Dr. Karadzic is telling him that, "No, we have to -- we have -- we have to proceed. We can't live with them any more and we --" indicates that, in fact, this -- this was part of -- one step in a plan that they had and they had to continue on that path.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tender 30379, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you referred to the establishment of the Serb autonomous regions in September of 1990 and now the establishment of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in October. Referring back to the autonomous regions for a moment, apart from identifying or aggregating territory as you indicated before, did the region serve any functional purpose at that time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, within the context of the emerging Bosnian Serb entity, yes. The Assembly was just that. It was an assembly. It was a legislative body, if you will. It did not have any executive organs. The only executive organs that the SDS leaders had at their disposal were the municipalities that they were in control of, which I indicated were the fundamental unit of local government in BH. But they had also created the Serbian autonomous districts, the SAOs, so they had -- they could use them as executive organs and as means of communication with lower-level governmental bodies as opposed to party bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a few documents next. The first would be 30400. This is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and General Simovic on the 2nd of November, 1991, and if we could turn to page 4 of both the English and B/C/S. And there Dr. Karadzic explains to General Simovic in the third paragraph from the bottom: "I gave the order. I gave the order to all the municipalities there and all the presidents of the municipalities. I gave the order. They introduced the command post. They also introduced the wartime, completely wartime -- wartime conditions of economy and work and all. I announced general mobilisation to them because it is ongoing from earlier on like I said," and so on. And if -- could you place that in context, please, and do you know what order Dr. Karadzic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This conversation is with Tomislav Simovic who was at that time the minister of defence of the Republic of Serbia. They're discussing the ongoing war in Croatia. The need for manpower for the army was a very important issue that Dr. Karadzic and the SDS got involved with in Bosnia, getting people -- Bosnian Serbs to respond to a call-up there or to volunteer to serve there. So that's what they're discussing, and the order that he refers to that he gave I believe we do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could tender 30400. Your Honour, I understand we'll go through the identification notation by Mr. Robinson so -- so if that could be marked accordingly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI P2547.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we turn next to 05410.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a telex. It refers to the Sarajevo SDS order brought to light at a meeting of all the mayors it says here, and you can explain what that is, Dr. Treanor. A meeting chaired by Dr. Karadzic. That order provides, number 1: "To form commands and institute permanent watch immediately to institute full mobility of the territorial army," and so on, and it bears the name at the bottom of the co-ordinator for implementation of decision, Radoslav Brdjanin the vice-president of the autonomous region Assembly. And if you could put this document in context, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, this is the -- the only version that we have of the order that I believe was being referred to in the previous conversation. As you can see, the language of this order tracks the language - I hope you can see from the English - it tracks the language of the conversation that Dr. Karadzic was having with General Simovic. Something else I would point out about this document is that right at the top it says it's an order of the SDS and was conveyed by Dr. Karadzic at a meeting of the presidents of municipalities, that was translated as "mayor." Municipalities had so-called presidents who were in fact the presidents of the councils, the Assemblies, of the municipalities. They also had Executive Committees which were the executive organs and the executive committees had presidents too. The president of the municipality was regarded as the top official. So this is a meeting of government officials, SDS government officials, getting an order from Dr. Karadzic, a party order, being transmitted by an official of the autonomous region of Krajina, which was one of the -- one of the SAOs. So we see here Dr. Karadzic using the -- the SAOs, in this case the ARK, the autonomous region of Krajina as a means of communication for orders to government officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tender 05410, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2548, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could look next at 65 ter 30392, a conversation between Mr. Brdjanin who you just discussed and his name appears in the previous document and Dr. Karadzic on the 31st of October 1991. And if we could turn to page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic says to Brdjanin: "Come on man. Do your job. Don't call me about every minor problem. I'm not your nanny. You have power in your hands and you have presidents of municipalities through whom you can exercise this power until we achieve autonomy. So you cannot -- you cannot call me about every detail. You should execute power vigorously and to the fullest. Not a single bird should be allowed to fly over Krajina and there must not be a shortage of men from Krajina for the army. You must establish all of that. I've seen what was written and sent. All that must be implemented. Take care of that. Call each and every municipality president and keep checking if it has been implemented and accomplished." And if you could place that in context, please, Dr. Treanor, of the issues that you've just been discussing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this conversation takes place a few days after the issuing of the order that we saw on the previous document, although a couple days -- in a couple days before the conversation with Simovic, and here we see Dr. Karadzic urging Radoslav Brdjanin to see to the execution of that order and indeed in general terms urging him to exercise the powers that he and other officials in that area do have. The interesting thing about Mr. Brdjanin in this context is that he is both -- both a government official and a party official. I'm sorry, he was both a -- a local governmental official. He was the president of the Executive Committee of the municipality of Celina. So he was a local president himself. He was also the deputy president of the Assembly of ARK, the autonomous region of Krajina, and as we saw in the previous document he was also the co-ordinator for the execution of decisions. So he had a bit of an executive function as well, and he was also a deputy, an SDS deputy, in the -- in the BH Assembly, and by this time a deputy in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And this is one of many conversations that -- that Dr. Karadzic had with -- with a broad range of officials, local officials, urging them to do what -- what they need to do in order to carry out instructions and to exercise their authority. Whether they be party officials or government officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger -- yes. Marked for identification or... yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P2549.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's time for the break now, Mr. Tieger, and we will rise and resume with Dr. Treanor at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, after the establishment of the SAOs, the autonomous regions, in September, were any steps taken to incorporate them into the emerging state structures of an anticipated Bosnian Serb Republic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Is this on? Yes. Yes. As discussed in -- in my report and the leadership study, I would mention just some of the milestones. In November 1991, after the Bosnian Serb plebiscite which voted overwhelmingly in favour of the Bosnian Serbs remaining in Yugoslavia, the Bosnian Serb Assembly verified the establishment of the autonomous regions, of five autonomous regions, and specified which municipalities and parts of municipalities were in them. On the 9th of January, 1992, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was proclaimed, again as mentioned in the report, and in that declaration it states that the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is composed of the territories of the SAOs and additional territories, not precisely identified but to include areas where the Serbs had been in a majority before the genocide of World War II. At this time, the Bosnian Serb Assembly was also drafting a constitution for the Bosnian Serb Republic and the existence of regions or districts as referred to in the contusion were included.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn next to another stage of the process as described in your report, and that is the Bosnian Serb -- in particular the Bosnian Serb leadership 1990 through 1992, 2536, P2536, and there at paragraphs 61 through 64 you address the instructions -- the 19 December 1991 instructions or the so-called variant A and B document. Can you tell us very quickly what the variant A and B document was and what its general purpose was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: The so-called A and B document is a set of instructions issued under the name of the Main Board of the SDS to apparently -- or one can infer to the SDS Municipal Boards. I say you can infer that because they relate to activities on the municipal level. They specify two different sets of actions which could be taken under -- or should be taken under certain circumstances, a stage one and a stage two, phase one and phase two type of thing, and it also made some slight variations in the types of actions that would be taken and the different phases according to the type of municipality, the municipalities being categorised into type A and type B: Type A being the municipalities in which the SDS held political power, that is in which they had the majority in the Assembly of the given municipality, and type B municipalities being municipalities in which the SDS was not in power but which nevertheless had a Serbian pop -- some sort of Serbian minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you refer generally to activities on the municipal level which the instructions direct municipal -- SDS municipal officials to take. What sorts of actions are encompassed by the variant A and B document, the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, such steps are specified as forming a Serbian Assembly for the municipality in those municipalities where the Serbs were in a minority establishing Crisis Staffs, establishing check-points, or establishing various types of physical and institutional control.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you find efforts by the SDS leadership, and Dr. Karadzic in particular, to monitor the progress and implementation of the 19 December instructions of variant A and B document?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned, Dr. Karadzic was very active in making sure that his instruction were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn to 30489, please. And in particular to page 3 of that document. This is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik, held on 21 December 1991. Turn to page 3 of the English as well. There's a reference at the top of the page by Mr. Krajisnik to the dissatisfaction with people from the Krajina, according to what he'd been told, with that Cizmovic. Dr. Karadzic, says: "All right then, until the Serbian new year and then we'll see." Then Mr. Krajisnik says: "How did the idea come up that we should co-ordinate this?" Dr. Karadzic, says: "You know what -- who will implement what we issued last night." Krajisnik, says: "This council of ministers." Dr. Karadzic, says: "But they can't run from municipality to municipality," then he continues, "They cannot run from municipality to municipality and say do this, do that, or that." Mr. Krajisnik, says: "He won't run either." Dr. Karadzic, says: "But he must run." Can you put this in context for us, please, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This conversation takes place on the -- on the 21st of December, 1991, as stated, which is a day after there was a big party meeting of the type that is discussed in the report, and I believe as discussed in the report that it was at this meeting that the instructions A and B were disseminated, and I would conclude from what happened after that that the word was in fact given that they should implement phase one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's reference here to Cizmovic and his running from municipality to municipality. Who was Mr. Cizmovic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Right. Now, the next day, on the 21st of December, a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly was held. That session named a council of ministers. Mr. Cizmovic was made a member of that Council of Ministers. His title was as co-ordinator for the SAOs. Mr. Cizmovic was from Banja Luka. Apparently people -- some people in Banja Luka didn't like him. He was a lawyer. I hope that wasn't the reason why. But from this conversation I would conclude that among his duties was going to be the monitoring and enforcement -- or enforcement of the implementation of the A and B document as well, which is a party document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at a few conversations with Mr. Cizmovic, then, and I would tender this -- tender 30489, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if it could be identification only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2550, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First turning to 30491, a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Cizmovic on the 21st of December, 1991. And if we could turn to page 2 of both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there toward the bottom of the page Dr. Karadzic states to

utterances.speaker: MR. CIZMOVIC
utterances.text: "The most important thing now in this very moment is that those papers, those --" And Cizmovic, says: "To the realisation." Dr. Karadzic, says: "Right. Right." And then continuing on to the next page in English but staying on the same page in B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic tells him: "You have a full authorisation to visit all our municipalities, including even those where there is no and all those there who are ours." And he continues: "They have to say what problems they are facing, and they would certainly hear good advice from you. As to how to ..." If you could place this conversation in context as you've been discussing, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well this, conversation takes place on the same day as the conversation with Mr. Krajisnik, that is the day after, I believe, the A and B document was distributed, and Dr. Karadzic is giving him, Mr. Cizmovic, some instructions on to -- how to carry out his task. I note that the reference is to going round to the municipalities rather than going to around the SAOs. So I conclude that he's referring to the execution of the A and B document. I would note that he -- he refers to going around to all our municipalities, our municipalities in where there isn't any, "our municipalities" would be the variant A municipalities and "where this isn't any" and "where we're not in control" would be variant B municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour, understanding the MFI --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- comment that would be made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2551, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turning next to 65 ter 30558, a conversation between Mr. Cizmovic and Dr. Karadzic on the 16th of January, 1992, and if we could turn to page 7 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At that portion of the conversation Mr. Cizmovic says to Dr. Karadzic: "I've talked to Bijeljina," and he continues, "they are prepared for full co-operation. It's the same with Northern Bosnia. I've prepared a small sort of questionnaire for them -- for all of them." Dr. Karadzic, says: "Uh-huh." Then Mr. Cizmovic, says: "What have they managed to do? How far have they come?" And continues, "To what extent are they prepared to implement the first level of the instructions?" And if you could place that conversation in the context that we've been discussing, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this conversation takes place several weeks after the previous conversation. It takes place after the proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in this conversation Mr. Cizmovic is reporting back to Dr. Karadzic on his activities. He mentions going to a particular municipality, and I would note the reference to the question, the question in his questionnaire about being ready to execute the first phase of the instructions. Again, I conclude that this is a reference to the A and B document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 30558, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2552.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can call up 30564, please, a conversation again between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Cizmovic, this time on the 22nd of January, 1992. And if we could turn to page 5 of the English and of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Cizmovic says to Dr. Karadzic that he's talked to Doboj, and then he continues: "It's going normally," et cetera, and then he says, "And say how far --" excuse me, "I said as I could not attend today that they should mark the problem and say how far they have got to mark the problem, to see what they can do for themselves." Dr. Karadzic, says: "And for experts to go to them when they can't deal with something." Mr. Cizmovic, says: "If it's something for us, we'll go. We'll set up a team." He continues, "It's the same situation with Bijeljina. I have finished that with them too. I've still got to see about Birac." And then turning to the next page it says Birac, Romanija, and Herzegovina. Dr. Karadzic says: "All right." And Cizmovic, says: "But I'll see to it that they -- that that should be finished within this short time too." And then continuing on page 7 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S, Mr. Cizmovic says: "Tonight we also established the Crisis Staff which will --" excuse me, "which will act when nobody can get together, when they can assemble more quickly." Dr. Karadzic, says: "Excellent." Mr. Cizmovic, says: "So that's working because the objective must be carried out, instructions must be carried out." And Dr. Karadzic, says: "Yes, that's right." And if you could place this in context as well.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: This conversation takes place about a week after the previous conversation, and again Mr. Cizmovic is reporting back to Dr. Karadzic on his activities. Again he mentions Bijeljina which is a municipality here. He also mentions Birac, Romanija, and Herzegovina which are regions. He was the co-ordinator for the SAOs so that he was also working on that level. I note the reference to the creation of a Crisis Staff and the fact that instructions must be carried out. Again I conclude that here he's referring to the A and B document and his activities in seeing to the execution of those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, your --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2553, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, your report also notes that at paragraph 64 that the second phase or stage or step of the 19 December instruction were activated by Dr. Karadzic at the 14 February -- 14 February 1992 extended meeting. The transcript of that meeting has already been received in evidence, so I don't want to spend time with it, that's P00012, but does it contain explicit references to that activation by Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The meeting on that day is another one of the large meetings of the type discussed in the report, similar to the meeting on the 20th of December, 1991. Dr. Karadzic makes reference to phase two several times in the course of his remarks to that meeting. He says, among other things, explicitly that you've been called together to activate phase two, and he links the activation of phase two with the passage of a resolution in the Bosnian Assembly, again in the absence of the SDS deputies, to hold a referendum on independence in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, with reference to these various stages or steps that you -- you've discussed concerning identifying or marking territory and ensuring control over those territories, toward the establishment of state structures and so on, did you find indications or reflections of whether these were thought up on the spot or planned in advance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, there are certainly indications that they were planned in advance in that connection, and I would note among other things that the -- the progression of the steps that were taken broadly speaking by the Bosnian Serbs were the same as those that were taken by the Croatian Serbs just a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn to P00953, please. And in particular to page 3 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. This is an interview of Dr. Karadzic in January of 1995 by "Srpsko Oslobodjenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And toward the bottom of the page in response to the question what about the Serbian Democratic Party's role in the political struggle, and then in the preparation and organisation of the Serbian people we see the passage from Dr. Karadzic: "We had a list of the actions and steps to take, but we always waited for the Muslims to make a mistake, and after they made one, we created a union of municipalities and the Serbian autonomous areas next, followed by the regions and eventually our Assembly, and finally republic." And can you place that in context and explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, well, this interview takes place almost three years after the Bosnian Serb Republic was proclaimed and -- gone on in the interval, which I won't get into, but here Dr. Karadzic is looking back and mentions the fact that they -- they had a plan, some steps laid out in advance, and that they -- they waited until the appropriate time to take each step. He was critical of the Croatian Serb leaders for the -- their timing, basically. The steps he lays out here are ones that were in fact taken by the Bosnian Serbs. I think we've -- we've mentioned them all. There -- there maybe other steps that he also had planned out in advance, but he certainly mentions these as being steps that they wanted to take and simply waited until the appropriate time, which he links to mistakes that the other side may make.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, as you noted this is 1995, and as Dr. Karadzic looking back and is a -- made in a public context, did Dr. Karadzic indicate the same thing earlier and in less public forms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we look at 06361, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Treanor, this document is a record of the meeting of the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia held on 9 December 1991. I'd like to turn to page 78 of the English and 106 of the B/C/S. There at the top Dr. Karadzic explains to those gathered: "We have to be wise enough and prepare both legality and the factual status." But I want to draw your attention to his comments in the next paragraph, and he states: "We have made a list of moves, ten moves in the direction we want so that there are results. Bosnia remains in Yugoslavia either as a whole or our areas, but we won't do anything until Alija messes something up. When Alija messes something up, we make move number five, and then we wait. When Alija messes something else up, we make move number six." He goes on to explain that they didn't make the move on the plebiscite prematurely which would have had an adverse effect and so on. And he concludes: "So we must all play the same strength." Dr. Treanor, can you place that in context of the issues we've been -- the issue we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. First let me say this is a meeting that was held at the Presidency in Belgrade. It is not a session of the Presidency in Belgrade, that is a formal session of that body, but a meeting between members of the Presidency, the currently active members of the Presidency, and a host of other Serbian leaders from Croatia and Bosnia, including Dr. Karadzic, and they're generally discussing the war, the situation there, and the efforts to come to peace, the Vance Plan, that type of thing. And here Dr. Karadzic is saying again that he had certain steps and -- in mind, and they waited for the right moment to execute each of those steps. He -- he makes reference to ten steps. Now, whether there are literally ten steps or whether he's just speaking sort of figuratively -- figuratively, I don't know, and again whether the five or six or -- exactly steps five and six, I don't know. But certainly the idea is that he -- they had a -- a plan to execute certain steps and waited for the right time to execute each one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 06361, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2554, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, with respect to this plan that Dr. Karadzic has outlined and the stages in which it would be implemented, did he communicate this to the field, to his -- to SDS officials in the regions and municipalities?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, he did, in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could we turn to 65 ter 30354, please. This is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Vukic, and Boro Sendic on the 16th of October 1991, and I'd ask to turn to page 2 of both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, there Dr. Karadzic, says after a generalised -- after a complaint they'd been isolated: "No way, you're not isolated at all. Can listen to press conferences, we're in touch over the phone, everything's going very well. Nobody has the right to leave the Serbs in Central Bosnia or in Semberija or in east Herzegovina high and dry. We have to pressure others. Now I have to say it, although they're listening in to the conversation, we have to pressure others into secession, because if we secede, we won't even get a third of what belongs to us." And then we could continue on page 6 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S. He states: "We'll come. We've worked out a scenario.
