We won't make a single move today, if necessary we'll do it tomorrow because it would be a great pity to do it today and tomorrow. It would be very useful. Everything's been worked out." And then continuing on the fifth entry from the bottom he notes a long meeting: "We had a long meeting that lasted five hours. We clarified many things there, purged. Of course, not the strategic secrets but hidden strategic things. We clarified everything." And then he notes: "We're working on the diary with precision, this move, that move, so that no one can do anything, man." And then finally the last entry of page 9 of the English and the final entry in the B/C/S as well, he notes: "There should and meeting with just a few of us. Some people will get assignments. We have a diary of events. We know exactly which should be made." And if you can place that in the context identifying the persons with whom -- or person Dr. Vukic and Mr. Sendic with whom Dr. Karadzic is speak and the timing.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, what Dr. Karadzic is speaking with Dr. Vukic, who is the SDS president of the municipality of Banja Luka. I don't know precisely who Boro Sendic is. I would infer that he's a local SDS official of some description. This conversation that takes place a day after the adoption of the memorandum by the Bosnian Assembly that I referred to that the Bosnian Serbs objected to so much, and he's in this -- in that portions of the conversation assuring Dr. Vukic, who is wondering what's going to happen now, that they do have a plan. They're in control of the situation. They just had a big meeting. As we know, they did have a meeting of the party council at that time. He obviously doesn't want to talk too much about this over the phone, but assuring Dr. Vukic that they do have a strategy and they're trying to stick to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 30354, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2555, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And -- and one more document I'd ask you to look at in connection with the communication of the steps and plans to the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to 30543. This is a conversation of January 11th, 1992, involving Dr. Karadzic and Nenad Stevandic, and if we could turn, please, to page 6 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just at what would be the beginning of the second half of that page Dr. Karadzic says to Mr. Stevandic: "Listen Nenad, well, they cannot. We have all of that in the plans. We have all moves in the envelopes. They must not do it before we do it in the whole of Bosnia. Why are they playing smart? They're explaining my policy to me." Then he goes on to talk about the plebiscite, and then he continues at the bottom of the page: "However, we are doing everything else. We will have a council of ministers today. There is -- we have done everything today. We have plans for everything. They just keep running ahead like oxen after salt. Let them stop for a while and let them synchronise their work with the party. " And if you could place that in context, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this conversation is with Nenad Stevandic who was an SDS member or supporter in Banja Luka. I'm not sure if he had any position at that time. He was later a member of the Crisis Staff in the autonomous region of Krajina, that this takes place a few days after the proclamation of the Bosnian Serb Republic, and he, Dr. Karadzic, is referring to the fact that there are - as [indiscernible] refer to them on a previous occasion - ad hocs within the party who would like to -- were straining it at the bit, to change the metaphor, wanting to run ahead. But no, we have plan and we have to do everything at the right time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the reference to the council of ministers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: That's a reference to -- the council of ministers that was appointed on 21st of December, and that council of ministers, I believe, met on this day or certainly around -- around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender 30543, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2556, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you've already discussed - and I know your report details the hierarchical nature of the SDS, and you've mentioned the emphasis on adherence to the policies and instructions of the central SDS leadership by lower levels. I wanted to ask you, we've seen some communications with officials in the field, but I wanted to ask you quickly more generally how were -- what -- what forms of communication were used for getting instructions and information to the field and information back on their implementation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, there were a variety of means that were available to Dr. Karadzic and the other top SDS leaders at this time. First of all, as discussed in the reports, they had many meetings of varying sizes, some including officials from all around Bosnia, both party officials and government officials who were SDS people. They could communicate by telephone. They could communicate by telex, as we've seen. And they could communicate by -- by letter, many of which were faxed, which was a technology available at that time. So they made use of, I think, of the range of technological capabilities that were available to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what role did Dr. Karadzic take in communicating with the field, either at the regional or municipal levels?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, looking at the totality of -- of the documents that -- that I've seen, not all of which are mentioned in the reports by any means, Dr. Karadzic seems to have been a very active leader, a very hands-on leader, if you will. He made -- he organised these large meetings on a fairly regular basis and made extensive use of the telephone in talking to leaders at various levels around the country, directly to municipal leaders and also to regional leaders of the SDS, talking to the highest level Bosnian Serb officials in the Bosnian government, that is members of the Presidency, members of the government itself, with Momcilo Krajisnik, of course, who was the president of the Assembly, and talking to Slobodan Milosevic and other people in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection in terms of communications with people in the field, can we turn next to 30058. This is a telephone conversation of the 24th of June, 1991, between Dr. Karadzic and Goran Babic. And if we could turn to page 3 of both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of references and I'll ask you to place it in context. There's a discussion about several people. In the middle of the page by Dr. Karadzic were mention of them: "All those people who made us problems cannot join the party now. That is my order. Tell them that I will introduce new measures in Prijedor and that I will tell them who the president will be there."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thing turning to page 4 of the English and I guess remaining at page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic states: "Tell him everything. Tell him that I will dissolve the board. I will place ten people to lead the party." And finally on the last page, Dr. Karadzic, says: "If you are not able to organise the real democratic elections without those bastards, I will name 10 to 15 people to lead it as I did last time." And if you could place that in context, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a conversation with Goran Babic who was an SDS man in Prijedor. I'm not sure what precise position he may have occupied there, but he's calling Dr. Karadzic because he's concerned about affairs in the party there, and here we see Dr. Karadzic giving him instructions on how the party should be organised and telling him that if they can't do it themselves, he'll do it for them basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2557, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn next to 65 ter 30328. This is a conversation of 8 October 1991 involving Dr. Karadzic and Brane from Visegrad. And if we can turn quickly to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Toward the second half of that page they're discussing a dead-line. Dr. Karadzic, says: "Give them seven days," and then continues toward the bottom of the page, "If not we shall proceed to organise parallel organs of power with a view to protecting the Serbian people. They should be told that openly and that's it, that's it." And Dr. Treanor, if you can place this conversation in context and of the communications made between the central level, the SDS, and particularly Dr. Karadzic, directly to the field.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this is a conversation with someone in Visegrad. There is an SDS official down there whose first name is Brane, who was reporting on a local matter, and again Dr. Karadzic is giving him instructions on how to handle the situation. They make reference to establishing their own police station down there. I would note that around this time in October 1991 there were discussions among the Bosnian Serb leaders about precisely that, establishing a separate Ministry of Internal Affairs for the Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2558, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As you noted, Dr. Treanor, those two communications were directly with municipal officials. Were policy -- were similar discussions regarding directions or policy from Dr. Karadzic also made to the regional level?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I think we've seen an example of that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could turn your attention to perhaps one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 30363.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a conversation of 18 October 1991 between Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Brdjanin who you discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn quickly to page 2 of the English toward the top, and that's the bottom of page 1 in the B/C/S moving on to the top of page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic states: "What do you mean we're not supporting you? We always do what is necessary and the way it should be done. We are always with you and constantly trying to calm things down. But look, you cannot refuse to come today because we're taking a decision that will be important for Europe and one which Europe will have to accept. Do you understand?" Brdjanin says: "Doesn't matter. I'm pursuing the policies from headquarters and they're being implemented here. But over the past month I've got the impression that they're fucking around, pardon my French, and no one is reacting." And then at page 3 of the English, I just wanted to bring your attention to this portion toward the second half of that page where Dr. Karadzic makes reference to the -- he says: "We are not a Communist Party that can simply remove someone by decree even though I have introduced a state of emergency. I don't know if you've received that information. Mr. Brdjanin, says: "Yes, of course I have." Dr. Karadzic, says: "The Municipal Boards must meet every day. We have to do this today." And can you place this conversation in context, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This conversation is a very interesting example of communications and indeed planning in the SDS. The conversation took place on the 18th of October. On that day Dr. Karadzic did proclaim a state of emergency in the party, something that Mr. Brdjanin was already aware of, and he -- Dr. Karadzic also refers to a meeting that was going to take place that day. This is a meeting in response to the adoption of the memorandum on the sovereignty of Bosnia a few days before, and this was the meeting at which the SDS leaders decided, among other things, to establish their own Assembly and to hold a plebiscite among the Serbs in Bosnia. He's insisting to Dr. -- Mr. Brdjanin how important that meeting is and that he attend it and he, in fact, did attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour. It's 30363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Again, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2559.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you mentioned the various ways of communicating with the field. Let me just look -- ask you to look quickly at 00949. This is a document dated the 15th of August, 1991, accepted by Dr. Karadzic, president of Serbian Democratic Party, operating instructions to all the SDS Municipal Boards, obligatory for everyone. It provides for meetings once a week, local boards to meet. Every member of a local board must be entrusted with maintaining the contact with 10 to 20 homes, the submission of information or report on the situation and the completion of a questionnaire. If you could place that in context, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, this document is an example of a different type of communication, in this case a letter or circular -- circular if you will, from the -- from Dr. Karadzic. The document does not have an original signature on it. It has -- does have a stamp of the SDS, however, and the letterhead of the SDS, the typed letterhead as they were accustomed to doing it at that time. Sent out to all the Municipal Boards and telling them that they should have regular meetings and -- on the municipal and local level and report back. So this is an example of a particular type of communication and one that demands communication from the -- the lower ranks the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender 00949, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2560, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Treanor, I'd like -- if I can move forward a few months to late March 1992 and look at another communication --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this was admitted yesterday. That it already bears a D or a P number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I think that may be right. I do recognise the document, so -- but that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. In any event, we think we have the document. I'd like to call up the 23 March 1992 document, which either bears 05420 or a new designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a strictly confidential, indeed must be destroyed after reading, document that bears Dr. Karadzic's name and signature and the seal, dated March 23rd. Can you explain what this document is -- refers to and its context, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this document was issued on the 23rd of March 1992, which is at a time when the Bosnian Serb leaders were activating their government structures. They had adopted a constitution on the 28th of February, 1992, and some legislation associated with that law and the government on ministries to flesh out that constitution, and on this date, in fact, they published some of those laws in their own gazette, their own "Official Gazette," and those laws would have come into effect according to their texts eight days later on the 31st of March, and they, in fact, had a ceremonial proclamation of the constitution of the republic on the 27th of March and elected a government as opposed to a council of ministers. The government now had a statutory basis in the laws that I had referred to. So this was a very active period for them in getting their structures, especially at the centre, activated, and Dr. Karadzic in this communication, which is again a written communication, is informing the municipal presidents of the establishment of a -- rather the perfection, if I can put it that way, of a communications system and that they should be aware of and will be able to use. I would note that he sends this document as the president of the party, which was the only position he occupied. He had no government position in the official structure of BH as opposed to many of the other leaders that we've been discussing, but he sends it to all presidents of municipalities. I would conclude that he's sending this to the presidents of Serbian municipalities since they were the only ones who were likely to obey the head of the SDS. So it's rather interesting from that point of view. We're seeing him again as -- as in the 26 October 1991 telex as party leader conveying instructions to government officials on a lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 05420 if it isn't already in evidence, but I guess that can be determined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was right as to the admission of the previous document and this will also be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous one is P2529, if that is of any assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That's P2529, and the current document which is 05420 will be Exhibit P2560.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you've spoken about - and I know detailed more extensively in your reports - the efforts to earmark territory through the process of regionalisation or the creation of Serbian municipalities and so on. We've now looked at a document that put us in late March 1992. Once the conflict began, did Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership take further steps to identify their priorities, and did those have territorial aspects?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They adopted at the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, which is a very important session. It changed some of the institutional structure of the republic at the top. They created a three-member Presidency and elected Dr. Karadzic to that Presidency and created the army and made General Ratko Mladic the commander of that army. Pursuant to a report by Dr. Karadzic on -- when he referred to as the strategic goals of the Serbian people, they adopted those goals. The first goal was the -- as detailed in my report --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And can I stop you for a second. You may be assisted if I could call up 19154.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 19154.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think it needs to be released, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that has now been released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Dr. Treanor, but I hoped this might be of assistance to you and to the Court as you continue with your response concerning what you were referring to, which is the adoption of the strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned, the strategic goals are -- as set out at this meeting are discussed in the leadership study. Indeed, Dr. Karadzic's speech on that occasion is extracted in verbatim at some length because I regard them as so important. This map quite neatly summarises them. The first goal as can be seen here is the separation of the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities in their own entity. The second goal, which is the arrow at the top in the middle, objective 2 is a corridor; in other words, a territorial connection between the area of Semberija on the east and Bosnian Krajina on the west. The corridor is a sensitive issue because the area of -- there are areas of Croatian settlement up there and Muslim settlement, and the corridor was necessary in order to -- to hold not only the Bosnian Serb Republic together, the east and the west, but also to make possible overland communications between Serbia and the eastern part of the republic -- the Bosnian Serb Republic with major portions of the Croatian Serb Republic, known as the Serbian Republic of Krajina, which had its capital in Knin, which is sort of just south around where you see the word "Una, objective 4," so in the white area around there. So it was a very important communications corridor that they wanted to have. The third is the Drina valley. The importance of the Drina valley to them is twofold. One is that was where the border with Serbia and the FR -- and Montenegro, the -- parts of Montenegro, the FRY was, and they wanted to have direct communication with those Serbian states and did not want to have any Muslim territory between them and the Serbs. Again, there was a lot of Muslim settlement in the Drina valley. Also the -- the -- a corridor, so to speak, would facilitate communication between Semberija in the north and Herzegovina in the south, which is around the area where you see on the map that says "Neretva, objective 4." The areas -- large areas of Muslim -- general Muslim population being in between those two areas, otherwise the corridor along the Drina was necessary for communication between them. Then the objective 4 was to establish a border on the Neretva. You can see that objective 4 in the centre. The bottom, the Neretva River, as indicated there, kind of twists around. I don't think they wanted to have their border on the whole course of it there, but basically the portion that runs from directly north to south from just south of Sarajevo to perhaps the sea. And then the Una is indicated, the Una River, objective 4, up on the top of the map on the -- on the left-hand side for large portion of that river which flows into the Sava, which is at the north and is not indicated as such on that map but basically the northern boundary of Bosnia is the Sava River. The Una forms the border with Croatia for some of its course and for other parts of the course, as you can see there, it runs through Bosnia. According to this objective, the Bosnian Serbs were not claiming the area to the north and the west of the Una. That's an area known as Cazin Krajina from the name of one of the principal towns there and that was a very heavily Muslim populated area. So they're not claiming that under this objective. And 5, as you can see Sarajevo is in the middle, to divide Sarajevo. And 6 would have been access to the sea. They don't specify exactly where, but it would have had to have been somewhere in the -- in the area of where the arrow is on the map but is where the Herzegovina -- Bosnian Serb Herzegovina is closest to the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated that these were -- these goals were articulated at a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992. Were they maintained throughout the course of the conflict through -- until it -- its conclusion in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, they were. These objectives underlay the position of the Bosnian Serb negotiators who were headed by Dr. Karadzic throughout all the negotiations that took place in relation to peace throughout the course of the war and going through the Dayton meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Turn -- I ask you to look at 65 ter 01344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you want the map admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an interview with Dr. Karadzic by Nevesinje in 1995, and if I could turn your attention, please, to page 3 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S, the bottom of the centre column. Dr. Karadzic states in response to the question about the western and southern borders being a hot topic in Herzegovina: "Is Herzegovina going to return to its historical Serb borders the Neretva River?" And Dr. Karadzic states: "Our Assembly has adopted six strategic goals of this war. Goal number 3 is the Neretva River as a border. The territory and the left bank of the Neretva is Serbian territory. We are not giving up on that and never will. We will seek to accomplish that through political or military means." And then he continues to discuss the thousands of Serbs who are now bravely fighting to defend the remainder of Herzegovina. Can you place that in context? Is that a reflection of what you were mentioning a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This interview was given in May 1995 at a time when there was probably some uncertainty, some anxiety among the people and the leaders of the Republic of Srpska. The Croatian forces had just on the 1st of May eliminated one portion of the RSK, that is the Croatian Serb entity in Croatia, which caused quite a shock among Serbs in both entities. In -- in this article we see Dr. Karadzic giving public assurances that the leadership is still adhering to the six strategic objectives that were adopted, and he discusses, here in particular, the two objectives that would be of most concern to people in Herzegovina; that is, the border on the Neretva, which had not been reached militarily at that time, and access to the sea, which is -- and also not been achieved by that time, either militarily or in any negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. That can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2562, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that was a document that reflects a public statement by Dr. Karadzic in respect of the strategic objectives. Let me first ask you, were reflections of the adherence to the strategic objectives made both in terms of explicit reference to the strategic objectives and -- or -- and also by references to individual goals encompassed by the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Sometimes you'll see references to the expression the strategic objectives as a whole or the very frequent discussion of -- varies of the individual objectives and how far that objective has or has not been obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn to 05321 please. This document reflects the minutes of a meeting on August 20th, 1994, between Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Milan Martic, the president of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to just quickly draw your attention to three references. The first on the bottom of page 5 in English and page 4 of the B/C/S. Where Dr. Karadzic states that: "Squeezing under the bridge in Brcko is no good. It's a tunnel, not a corridor. Under this scenario you would be surrendered because we would be unable to help you. Everything would be controlled." And then turning to page 6 and page 4 of the B/C/S, there is a reference to the -- a concern about the vulnerability of the Kljuc-Jajce road which can easily be severed. And finally on the next page, page 7 of the English and still on page 4 of the B/C/S, the reference: "The maps are unacceptable. The eastern enclaves are unacceptable." And can you very quickly place that in context of the strategic objectives -- discussion and continued adherence to the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This meeting took place shortly after a break in relations between the Republika Srpska and the FRY had taken place over the -- the rejection of the so-called Contact Group Plan by Republika Srpska. A map had been presented by the so-called Contact Group in July, and the parties were asked to accept it or reject it as -- and the other parties accepted it, but the Bosnian Serbs did not. They offered to continue negotiations but did not accept the map. And here Dr. Karadzic, in a meeting with the president of the RSK, which supported the Serb position in this case, is giving a bit of a rundown on their objections to the map in -- in terms of the strategic objective -- objectives. The reference to the tunnel in Brcko that relates to the corridor, he notes that they're being offered something very, very narrow up there which is very important for them and also for the RSK as a route for communications, and such a narrow corridor would not be -- would not be adequate or wouldn't be defensible, that type of thing. Then he mentions the Kljuc-Jajce, that area. That area relates to the border on the Una which that map did not concede to them. It gave the Muslims fairly extensively territory just on the east side of the Una. And then the reference to the enclaves is -- is interesting, because in 1992, in laying out the objectives as quoted in my report, Dr. Karadzic at that time has said that such enclaves might be acceptable. Here he's indicating that they're unacceptable, although on other occasions he -- around this time he said that, well, maybe they would be. So a bit of a -- a bit of waffling on that point, but again laying out his position on that proffered territorial settlement in terms of individual objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour. I tender 05321.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2563, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And very quickly Dr. Treanor, I just wanted to -- on the subject of the last document 01363. I wanted to move ahead just slightly and -- this is now July of 1995, an interview with Dr. Karadzic in El Pais, and I just want to draw your attention quickly to two references there. First of all at the bottom of page 9 of the B/C/S, after the comment above "Our number one priority is to form part of Serbia," it continues to the very bottom of the page in response to the question: "What's wrong with that plan?" Answer: "First of all, we now have a state in one piece with contiguous territories." And then it goes on to describe what the problems may be with the plan not fulfilling that. And finally turning to page 12 in e-court, question: "What is your view on the future of Sarajevo." Answer: "Sarajevo will be transformed into two cities, two neighbouring cities if the Muslims wish. Otherwise, a Serbian city because the city was built in a Serbian zone." And again, do these remarks reflect continuing adherence to the strategic objectives as you've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see Dr. Karadzic referring again to two specific objectives, one to do with -- with the Drina, noting that the enclaves are not viable and must disappear. I think further down in the interview he -- I think he expresses a little bit more flexibility on that particular issue, and then of course the other thing he discusses here is the future of Sarajevo which was one of the objectives and indicates continued adherence to that objective, dividing Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2564, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Treanor, you talked about Dr. Karadzic's role in the party. I wanted to ask you quickly about his position in the formal structures of Republika Srpska once -- once it was established. May I ask you first of all whether his position as the top person in the SDS was translated into his assumption of positions in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I -- I would say that -- I'm not sure what "describe" has been translated into but, rather, in addition to his position as party leader which he continued to be and continued to be important. The first official position that we -- we see him occupying is as president of the so-called National Security Council which was established by the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 27th of March, 1991, just in a period that I mentioned when they were activating their central organs. Without going into too much detail because it's explained in the reports, that National Security Council acted as a supreme executive body for the Bosnian Serb Republic for a short time, sort of a central Crisis Staff. Dr. Karadzic came as the president of that council. It included the two acting presidents of the republic and members of the government, and they met fairly frequently during April and early May to consider the situation and adopted many decisions in connection with the establishments of the republic and the prosecution of the war. I have -- on the 12th of May, as I mentioned, the Assembly made some changes to the -- to the structure of the Presidency. Again, without going into too much detail because it's detailed extensively in the report, they created a temporary three-man Presidency, elected Dr. Karadzic to that Presidency along with Drs. Plavsic and Koljevic who, at their first meeting on the same day, elected him president of that Presidency, that Presidency was expanded to the five people at the beginning of June, 1991, to include the prime minister Dr. Djeric and the president of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik. Then on the 17th of December, 1992, the Assembly again changed the temporary structure by temporary -- I mean pending the holding of elections under the constitution which they say could only happen after the war was over. They created a -- a single president and elected Dr. Karadzic to that position and elected Drs. Plavsic and Koljevic as vice-presidents. Now all of those bodies that I mentioned - excuse me - exercised the powers of the office of the president of the republic. In the constitution and the legislation that was passed those powers are specified. Again very briefly because this is laid out in -- in the report and in the addendum to the report, the president of the republic was the Commander-in-Chief of the army, commanded the army in war and peace, and gave -- specified a wide range of duties and responsibilities for the president, including disciplinary powers, powers of appointment of officers, and also created the position of -- that is, legislation created the position of the commander of the Main Staff of the army. That would be the top uniformed professional officer. However, according to the legislation, that official, that officer, only had such authority as the president as Commander-in-Chief granted to that officer. So the president of the republic was the Commander-in-Chief in name and fact, and Dr. Karadzic was very active in exercising his powers and authority as Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we'll take the second break now, and we will resume sitting at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, just before we adjourned, you had been referring to Dr. Karadzic's position as Commander-in-Chief or supreme commander of the military forces of the Bosnian Serbs, including his very active role in exercising those powers, and you also alluded to the position of commander of the Main Staff. Your report also contains references to some friction between Dr. Karadzic, the supreme commander and General Mladic, the head of the Main Staff. And I wanted to direct -- ask you about a couple of documents in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the first is 65 ter 0657 -- 06507. Excuse me. Now, this document contains -- it is dated August the 5th. It contains an interview of Dr. Karadzic with Bosnian Serb television on August the 4th, 1995, and with Dr. Karadzic explaining a number of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, are you familiar with this document, and can I ask you to put it in context for us, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I use this document in the leadership study. This is an interview that took place on the -- late in the evening of the 4th of August in connection with Dr. Karadzic's reorganisation of the top military command structure in Republika Srpska and the removal of General Mladic as commander of the Main Staff and making him an advisor to the -- to himself as supreme commander. That came as a bit of a shock to everybody. The interview itself and all this is taking place at a time when military developments on the ground were progressing rather rapidly. There had been some successes and defeats by the Bosnian Serb forces, and on this very day Croatian forces launched their Operation Storm directed against the remaining portions -- the major remaining portions of the RSK, including toward the -- their capital of Knin, many of those operations being based in areas of Bosnia that the Croatian forces had recently taken. So it was a period of some military crisis. It was also potentially a period of political crisis in that Mr. Milosevic had come out publicly on the 1st of August, as detailed in my report, sending letters, almost identical letters to General Mladic, interestingly, and President Izetbegovic saying that now is the time to shift from military to political means and to start negotiating peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Does Dr. Karadzic in this interview in explaining his effort to reorganise the -- to conduct this reorganisation, does he praise certain commanders or events and criticise others?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he mentions some of the successes and some of the defeats, and he named certain commanders, noting that it wasn't their mistake that led to those defeats, by implication blaming General Mladic. In -- in this interview, Dr. Karadzic shows every intention of pursuing the military struggle in the sense that he's carrying out this reorganisation in order to improve the efficiency of the military commander, including vis-a-vis the forces of the RSK and their co-operation with those of the RS, those two entities having formed several months previously as detailed in my report a joint defence council. So there is a certainly very strong applied criticism here of the performance of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 06507.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2565, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to 04106, which is a document dated 5 August 1995, the subject matter of which is seen from the heading; that is, the same issue which is signed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Dr. Treanor, are you familiar with this document? Does it refer to the same issue that you've just discussed, and can you place it in context for us?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, this document is General Mladic's response to the action of Dr. Karadzic in removing him from his post as commander of the Main Staff. In this letter he in turn implicitly criticises Dr. Karadzic for his handling of military affairs, including operational affairs, and says that the move that he's just taken will undermine the military efficiency of the Army of Republika Srpska. He indicates that this is taking place at a time when Serbian unification, military and state unification had not yet taken place. He seems to regard that step as being detrimental to that effort, and whoever he -- General Mladic, in pointing out the successes and strengths of the RS, notes that -- of the Army of RS, that any army had created all the preconditions to end the war by political and diplomatic means. Now, this is sort of in line with -- not sort of. It is in line with what Mr. Milosevic was suggesting, indicating that there may have been some disagreement at this point between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic as to the desirability of continuing military operations to achieve their goals as opposed to switching to political means and engaging in peace negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender 04106, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2566, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally I turn to 06182, please. This is document dated 23 August 1995. It's a note from the 42nd session of the Supreme Defence Council held on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At page 5 of the English and 6 of the B/C/S, we see a reference toward the second half of the page to General Mladic being asked whether -- asked to state whether he would accept a solution negotiated by President Milosevic, and General Mladic stating that he did not wish to state his opinion explaining by the fact that he is only a soldier of the people. And then again at page 7, General Mladic stating he did not wish to contribute to a split in the Serbian people. And further down toward the bottom of the first half the page, refusing to sign a document stating that on behalf the Army of the Republika Srpska Main Staff he'll accept the peace plan reached by President Milosevic in Geneva. Dr. Treanor are you familiar with this document? Can you place it in context of the issues we've been discussing, please?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is a meeting that was held in Belgrade a couple of weeks after the exchange of correspondence that we've seen. Events have continued to take place. I would just mention in particular the -- in that regard the success of Operation Storm by this time eliminating -- virtually eliminating the RSK as a factor in the conflicts. This is a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY which is a body that was established under the constitution, the FRY to act as the supreme commander of the Armed Forces of the FRY. General Mladic, of course, among other things was a general in the -- in the -- in the army of the FRY. And we see him here being pressed by the FRY political and indeed -- and military leadership to support Mr. Milosevic's desire to negotiate peace at this point. Mr. Milosevic was already in contact with Ambassador Holbrooke who was attempting to organise such an effort. And we see General Mladic refusing rather loyally to his political leadership in Republika Srpska to -- to come out in favour of that and -- and suggesting that they have a broader meeting to include the political leadership of the -- of Republika Srpska so that they can consider that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2567, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Treanor, you spoke earlier in your testimony about the strategic objectives and their continued adherence, and you've just described what factors were at issue in the tensions that arose between Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic in August of 1995. In either these documents or in any other documentation is there any indication that Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic disagreed about the strategic objectives and the need to implement them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen any indication that they disagreed about the goals of the conflict, broadly understood as the unification of all Serbs or individually the strategic objectives. General Mladic, at the 16th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 12th of May 1992, when the objectives were adopted, had spoken out in favour of adopting precise objectives. He, subsequent to that session, issued a number of orders, military orders, for operations to pursue various of those objectives. He was perhaps, and I say perhaps and emphasise perhaps, even -- even more radical, if I can put it that way, than Dr. Karadzic and the other Bosnian Serb leaders as expressed in the objectives in -- in the military objectives that he would like to -- would have liked to see achieved. Dr. Karadzic made reference at one time in the Assembly, I believe, saying that General Mladic wanted to take the whole of Bosnia, and Dr. Karadzic replying that that's impossible. We have to leave room for the other people who live here. And -- and then General Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic was a bit critical at one meeting, I believe of the Supreme Defence Council, saying what General Mladic had said about anyplace that a Serbian soldier had set foot should remain Serbian was not correct. Now, those are statements from other people, that's not from General Mladic's mouth, but certainly I don't see anything that would suggest that he did not support at least the strategic objectives and the unification of all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Milosevic's interest in negotiating peace at that point. What sorts of pressures was Milosevic under, if any, in connection with ending the conflict, either political or financial?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, at this time, indeed for quite some time, the FRY was under tremendous economic pressure. Sanctions had been in effect since 1992 and gradually tightened. They were having -- and they were having their effect on the -- on the -- on the economy, in the -- the FRY and the situation in society, their living standards, inflation. And specifically the situation was very acute, indeed it had become acute a year before in relation to the capability of the FRY to continue giving military supplies to Republika Srpska. Even by the middle of 1994, they were -- they were running so low on ammunition and other equipment that that presented a threat to their military security and the capabilities of their own armed forces. Their stocks had been run down to way below to where the FRY military people thought it safe, and at that time, in the middle of 1994, they were resolved that they wouldn't be able to give -- just give things to the Republika Srpska any more, that they were going to have to buy them so that they could be manufactured because they just -- nothing existed that they could give them, that it would have to come out of new production. And this is before the break in relations in August of 1994, in relation to the Contact Group Plan. So there was going to be a scaling back on the aid from FRY in any case. Now, a year later that situation was not any better because the FRY was not able to replenish its own stocks and was in no condition - as the top FRY military people made clear to the political leadership at meetings of the Supreme Defence Council - it was in no condition to conduct a war and that therefore they had to seek peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as part of the -- just -- I know some of this is in your report, so I don't want to get into extensive detail, but as part of the military assistance provided by Serbia to the Republika Srpska, did that include salaries for officers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned before, General Mladic was, in fact, an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia, and thousands of other officers in the Army of Republika Srpska were also officers in the Army of Yugoslavia. As well as some non-commissioned officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was that referred to by the FRY leadership as part of the financial burden on them, that -- in the context of their desire for end of the war.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, it was a burden on them, but I don't think that was the main problem they had, but it was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you spoke about the strategic objectives. Was the continued adherence to the strategic objectives a factor that played a role in the ongoing negotiations that took place between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. The negotiations in that period basically turned on two issues. There were territorial issues, and that -- the strategic objectives from the point of view of the Bosnian Serb negotiators, they sought to achieve or confirm those objectives as far as they could. And if territorial settlements that were offered did not satisfy at least the most important of those objectives, they rejected them. The other set of issues was the nature of whatever central authority might be established in BH for the three communities. They were very insistent that that authority be weak, that their own authority be as strong as possible, that -- that they were in favour of basically a confederation, which in their conception, in the Serbian conception, confederation was not a state. They wanted the Bosnian -- the unified Bosnia to be as weak as possible at the centre, not to be unitary but to be such a confederation so that their entity would be able to associate with the other Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about a particular paragraph in P2538, your report on Radovan Karadzic and the Serbian leadership. That's paragraph 326, and there you're recounting comments at the 47th session of the SDC by Mr. Milosevic in December of 1995 about Dayton, and in the course of that, as for the latter half of -- first did -- Mr. Milosevic talks about what was entered into the books via Dayton, and then he recounts what he said years earlier to the -- about what was happening in Republika Srpska, and the quote you have here is: "I told them that two years ago. Dear gentlemen, you should stop thinking about what you want and think about what belongs to you. More than half of BH does not belong to us Serbs. More cannot belong to us because we constitute a third of the population. More than half is not rightfully ours. You must not take what belongs others." And then he continues: "From Zvornik to Foca, nowhere along the Drina was there a Serbian majority, and they took all of that. Or up there, Posavina, nowhere did you have a Serbian majority. Mladic said two days ago, we are not going to give what belongs to the Serbs. Sarajevo belongs to the Serbs." And he ends the quote in quoting Mladic, and then Milosevic continues: "If you please when, in this century were Serbs a majority in Sarajevo? When?" Dr. Treanor, are those references, the reference from Zvornik to Foca and nowhere along the Drina or the reference to the Posavina or the reference to Sarajevo, are those references to the strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Those are references to strategic objectives that we've -- as we've seen before, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And are those comments a reflection of the continued adherence of the Bosnian Serb leaders to the strategic objectives throughout the course of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly indicates that in Milosevic's view they were anxious to achieve those objectives. He seems to be -- have his own views about how important some of them might be or had justified, but he certainly indicates that those are the objectives they were pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Dr. Treanor, I wanted to go back to a comment you made --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I have to intervene. There are too many leading questions. This is a Prosecution witness, and my learned friend Mr. Tieger is not right to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, there's a difference between an expert witness who is giving evidence in accordance with their reports and their expertise and a witness who is giving evidence as to a fact. The reality is that even if the questions are to some extent leading, the witness will be entitled to give that evidence even if it was asked in a different form, and the evidence is patently coming from the, as it were, the intellect and opinion of the witness rather than derived from the question. So Mr. Tieger will be well aware of the differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to return now very quickly to a comment that you made earlier in -- and -- about an issue that was raised earlier, and that was the demographic concerns. We first saw demographic concerns expressed in the political council meeting exhibit that we saw. You then mentioned that Dr. Karadzic himself made comments on more than one occasion reflecting those demographic concerns, and if I recall correctly, I think you referred to the Assembly. So I just wanted to ask you about one Assembly session and the comments by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This would be the 37th Assembly session held on 10 January 1994, which is P1385, 01385, and I'd like to turn to page 107 of the English and 79 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is Dr. Karadzic speaking, and if we look at the second paragraph in the English at the bottom -- toward the bottom of page 107 he says: "We can consider ourselves as winners after occupying this land since the land is 100 per cent Serbian now. Therefore, even if we come down to around 50 per cent, we should be more than happy and satisfied, it is Dusan's empire." And then continuing on to the next page of the English. There is a discussion of various percentages. These 33.3 per cent have to be given to them now, and for the 44 per cent of the Muslims plus those 2 to 3 per cent of the population who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, it is too little." He continues in that paragraph: "In some ways the European Community accepts this, but they say give us Novi Prijedor, Sanski Most, all the way to Kljuc, the Sana River valley, give us the places where we were in the majority. We say we cannot give that. We were in the majority there before the Second World War, and then the European Community says that's -- that's history. Don't mention that now." And then finally turning to the next page in English, page 109, I believe that's page 83 of the B/C/S. Dr. Karadzic says: "The only thing we could do is say to Muslims: 'Gentlemen, Muslims, let us take piece of land from Croats and you can stay with us in Yugoslavia.'" And then he continues: "You cannot have it all. It is not the same time to have 24 to 25 per cent of Muslims in Nevesinje. The 23 per cent would rise to 24 per cent the day after, and the day after that one it would be 25 per cent, because that is how it is with them. They were 50 per cent of them and now they are gone." Dr. Treanor, is that one of the references to the ongoing demographic concerns that you referred to in your earlier -- in the earlier part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, the last part about the population in Trebinje is one of the things that I had seen. The earlier part that you read out, an interesting reference to areas where genocide had been committed and their continued desire to have -- have those areas. But the last part is certainly the type of thing I was thinking of. The other type, another example would be from the session of the deputies' club on the 28th of February, 1992, where there was extensive discussion of a move that was afoot in -- in Bosnian Krajina to declare their own republic, perhaps join the RSK, and, among other things, Dr. Karadzic said in that connection, I believe, that that would be a foolish thing to do because rather quickly the Serbs in that area would be outnumbered by the Muslims and it would turn into a Muslim state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before we go into any further detail, I would like to clarify the nature and the origin of your engagement. How was it that you took this job? How were you engaged for this job initially?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I'll briefly explain my connection with this institution. As I noted at the beginning of my testimony, I worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for many years investigating cases of alleged Nazi war criminals living in or seeking entry to the United States. I worked there for almost 14 years beginning in 1980. After our office was established, a new office in Washington to do precisely that, within a few years other countries had established similar offices to do -- to do the same thing. They were countries such as the United States, which were destinations for large numbers of refugees and other immigrants after World War II, referring in particular to Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom. We worked very closely with those offices. I had worked with the members of the Australian office. I knew Graham Blewitt, and he knew me at least by name and reputation. When this office -- when this institution was established, I was very interested in being associated with it given my background in investigating war crimes and in my knowledge of the particular area. Therefore, I wrote a letter to Graham Blewitt offering my services, and he was kind enough to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long did you work as an investigator of this Tribunal -- or, rather, of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by an "investigator." Technically, that is a functional title in the Office of the Prosecutor. I think when I came on board I was -- my contract said investigator. I was quickly made a -- with some other people made an operations officer. Then they had an exercise called classification, which is part of the UN personnel system in which they, "they" being the management of OTP and the Tribunal, made up job descriptions of the types of positions that they needed and the numbers of people, et cetera. It was at that time that they came up with a job description for something called a research officer, which I -- I think I had to reapply, sort of technically. But anyways, that was in about 19 -- I think 1997 that that whole drill was going on. So then I became a research officer, and that's what I remained for the rest of my stay at the Tribunal. I was always doing more or less the same type of work. So that would be 15 and a half years in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to your own statement given to the International Tribunal on the 27 January 2004, and in that statement you confirm that in your capacity as a team leader for research or investigations that you oversaw -- you visited the Republika Srpska on two occasions, in December 1997 and January 1998. Is it correct that you did indeed visit the Republika Srpska, and is it also true that the government of the Republika Srpska opened all of their archives to you and that you were able to pick and choose any of the documents you were interested in?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, I did visit Pale at that time. We were given extensive access to documents at that time. I would not say that it was unfettered access. We had access to a lot of things, enough to keep us busy, but certain things seemed to be missing. I can go into that detail if you wish. We were also -- among the things we were given access to were the records of the Presidency of RS, but it was made clear to us that they were only going to be available for a very short time, and we could take what we wanted by way of copies from those records, but once we'd had our -- our chance, it would not recur, and it was our feeling that there were also gaps in those records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to make my questions brief and allow you to answer them by just "yes" or "no." Do you agree at that moment in Republika Srpska it was the government of the Serbian Democratic Party that was in power?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: At the time I was there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you engaged as an expert? When did that moment occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, that's a very interesting question. As I think everyone in the -- in the courtroom is aware, there -- there is a practice among courts around the world to use experts of various types in -- in various types of trials, and indeed in the United States, in the course of our litigation on war crimes, we used experts to testify at trial. Now, it's the practice in the United States to use outside experts. That is, people who do not work for the Prosecution. I work for the Prosecution. That is the practice in the United States, and maybe in other countries. At this institution, when the need started to arise for such experts to testify at trial, the same approach was taken, perhaps under the impact of Anglo-Saxon practices. However, as the effort to collect documents, which I described briefly earlier in my testimony, proceeded, and we accumulated very, very large volumes of documents on an ongoing basis over a period of years and were conducting ongoing analysis, and I would emphasise in that regard myself and the people in my team always worked with the original documents, documents in the original language and not translation, so we were in a position to immediately work with documents once they had been obtained, that as a practical matter, it would not be possible to engage an outside expert to write a meaningful report based on those documents. It was felt by management, not by me, although I had to agree with it, that such an individual would have to come -- come here and spend months and months reading documents and writing a report. It was, on the one hand, virtually impossible to find somebody who was an expert in the field, people who are usually professors at universities, who was going to have that kind of time on the one hand, and on the other it was going to cost -- it would have cost a lot of money to do that, to do something that somebody working in OTP could do. So for those two very practical reasons, they decided to adopt the practice of using so-called inside experts. So that's how I became an inside expert, and I submitted the first report under my name in connection with the Krajisnik case and testified in that case and have done so since in other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you when and you answered as if I'd asked you why. Nevertheless, it is useful. How did you testify in the Brdjanin case, in what capacity, that is? And that was even before the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. You're absolutely -- absolutely correct. That was the first time I testified as an inside expert. When you said engaged as an expert, I was already engaged. I was already working for OTP, so there was no, you know, question of an engagement. It was -- it was just a development of my job description.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because we have had Prosecution witnesses who are also investigators and they testified as investigators. We've never had a case like yours before. And you describe your engagement as a necessity, because any other choice would have been more expensive and more difficult. For example, here in the -- 1D3522 is the number of the document. A Judge David asked you -- while we're waiting for the exhibit, 1D3552, in the introduction to your document 12125, which already has a P number, under item 2 or in paragraph 2 you state that you were given a task from the OTP. What precisely was your task that you were given by the OTP? What were you supposed to do for them? Could you please be as brief as possible. I asked for 40 hours for my cross-examination, and I was given barely one-fourth of that time, so I would kindly ask you to be as brief as possible in your answers.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, the task I was given by OTP in connection with these reports is set out in the copy of the letter that I received from Mr. Tieger, which you'll find on the second page of the addendum in the leadership study. The -- there was no such letter in connection with the earlier report. Procedures were a little bit different then, but the task was analogous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP give you an objective or something that you were to look for and establish? If you look at this transcript that is now in front of you, did you have a set of objectives that you were supposed to achieve in your work? No, this is not the correct page. Could you please first answer my question. Were you given a set of objectives or an objective at the same time when the OTP gave you your research or investigation task?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, again in connection with these reports, I would point to the letter that I'm referring to. That was -- those were the instructions, or the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 14 in this document. Line 20. I would like to draw your attention to lines 17 through 20. Judge David asks you whether you were given any objectives for your research, and you confirm that you were indeed given some objectives or goals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes. Broadly speaking in the sense of the contents of the letter. They ask for a report on a certain topic. They just don't ask for a report. I could write a report about anything. So the -- what's being referenced here are the type of guidelines or requests that is contained in the letter from Mr. Tieger. Also, there might be certain goals or whatever frequently in these conversations to do with the length of the report and that type of thing, and the dead-line by which it's due, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted into evidence, page 14 in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's part of an official transcript, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just briefly look at 1D3551.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These reports were created while you were still affiliated with the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed that also in another case. Can we look at page 599 in this document, please. Page 599. In e-court. Lines 13 through 22. You were examined and asked the following: "[In English] Well, your report -- after all, the report has been introduced and refined over many years, again it hasn't been produced in a vacuum. It has been produced by you working for the OTP," and [Interpretation] so on and so forth, and you answered, "Yes." Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, again, the same applies. It can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1258, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is true that you also interviewed witnesses on behalf of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I was present during a few witness interviews, including one with Mr. Krajisnik. I never conducted an interview independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever put questions to the witnesses during the interviews that were conducted by others?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, on occasion, including the interview of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you assist other OTP officials on various occasions and under various circumstances, and also, did they assist you in producing this report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, let me address the report. I think I've said that other members of my team assisted, broadly speaking, and I suppose there probably were other people involved in those collection efforts of the documents and that kind of thing. In preparing the report, I drew on -- I had the benefit of the work of any number -- a number of people. In that regard, I think most -- most -- all if not all -- most if not -- almost all if not -- actually, all the analysis was done -- analytical type of work was done by myself or members of my team under my direction. Have I helped other people in OTP? Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the introduction you say that the primary goal of this description is to enable the realistic and correct understanding of a -- the broader context in which allegedly Karadzic and other Bosnian Serb leaders participated in the large-scale violation of the humanitarian law in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Did the OTP suggest that you should take into account or perhaps not the conduct of other belligerent parties, and would the broader context mean that you should look at the conduct of the Serbs within the context of the conduct of other parties in the area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, for the purposes of these reports, you've seen the request and the guidelines that were given to me, I could say in addition to that that members of my team have done work on all the parties to the conflicts, and some of them have testified in other cases involving other parties to the conflicts. It was never suggested to me, as I think I made clear in my introductions to these reports, nor did I seek to write anything like a complete history of the conflicts. What you're suggesting is indeed very interesting, and I hope some day somebody will do that, drawing on the voluminous documentation that this Tribunal has been able to obtain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 1 of your introduction of the document, 12125, you say it's about primarily the objectives of the Serbian leaders, especially Radovan Karadzic, and then the course of the whole process and the extent to which these objectives were reached. So I wonder if it's possible to appraise the objectives of Radovan Karadzic if only one conduct is studied. How would you be able to assess a boxing match if -- if you were looking at a split picture, a split image seeing only one of the boxers? He would seem as if he was fighting with the air, flailing his arms around.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I agree with what you're saying. I just have to say that I think what you're suggesting is the job of this Court. The job that I was given is specified in the letter that I've been indicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are very fair in your introduction in saying that this document is not complete. Could you perhaps tell us if anyone was -- is dealing with this, and can we hope for a complete report any time soon?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's paragraph 4, where you say although these facts certainly don't represent a complete picture of the conflict in the area, the report does not pretend to be a comprehensive history of the political and other conflicts, let alone of those that engulfed the whole of the former Yugoslavia. Don't you think this Trial Chamber deserves to get a comprehensive history?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'll leave that to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's not really a question, Dr. Karadzic. It's a subject for a debate, and as you rightly pointed out, you have nine hours. I think it might be more efficient to move on to more specific questions, and perhaps it's a matter for you, but more closed questions so that you're likely to enable Dr. Treanor to give a more closed, precise answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll do my best, but I hope that the Trial Chamber will reconsider the time given me for this precious witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 78 of today's transcript, the examination-in-chief, lines 19 and 20, you discussed democratic changes in Trebinje. What was the reason for those changes - I'm speaking only of Trebinje - if you have managed to establish that? How did the Muslim share of the population in Trebinje change? How did it occur?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure which document was being discussed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On today's transcript, page 78, lines 19 and 20, you said: "Demographic changes occurred in Trebinje." Did you mean some artificial demographic changes such as ethnic cleansing or such? In any case, you found certain demographic changes to have taken place?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure what's being referenced. I'm sorry, I don't have transcript in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 19: [In English] The last part about population in Trebinje is one of the things that I had seen. The earlier part that you read out an interesting reference to the -- to areas where genocide has been committed and their continued desire to have these areas." [Interpretation] Do you remember mentioning Trebinje in this context?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Yes, actually, Mr. Tieger mentioned Trebinje. I remember the passage now and that was a passage that I had, of course, read before. I don't know precisely how those changes took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we -- can we see 1D471 for a moment. I want to know if you have seen this document before and whether you've taken it into account. P471 -- no, it's D471. It's been already admitted. Are you familiar with this instruction for evacuation from Trebinje sent by the SDA party on the 20th January, 1993, under the name of Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall having seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you then please look at it now to see the reasons and the ways of gaining a complete picture of the situation in Trebinje, and I would appreciate it if we could see in the original the name of the sender and the signature. Do you agree that in order to assess the events and the conduct of the Serbian side one would need to see this document from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is this looks like a very useful document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go together with you through your report and look at some of its conclusions. Page 4 to begin with of the 65 ter document 592. Maybe we don't need to show it, because's it's a well-known document, but I'd like to draw your attention to 65 ter 5912. It already has a P number, namely the executive summary. I don't need to read it, but it says the Serbian leadership, through the Serbian Democratic Party actively undermine the existing political system. And then on page 12, paragraph 4, we read that this report is to give a factual description of the army of the Bosnian Serbs and its political structures with special focus on the organisational steps taken by this leadership to ensure control over territories in an internationally recognised Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then paragraph 287 on the same document where it says that in October, the Serbian leadership began to undermine the joint state, et cetera, et cetera. And page 94, paragraph 165, where it says that Serbian deputies walked out of the Assembly. And now would you please look at another document, 12125, written for this case on the same subject, paragraph 68 -- "[In English] Karadzic's faith in Izetbegovic, however, was destroyed on 15th of October, 1992." [Interpretation] "Karadzic's faith in Alija Izetbegovic was destroyed on the 15th of October, 1992, and that session when the declaration on independence was adopted." And finally document 65 ter 592, page 62, paragraph 95, where it says that: "The SDS leadership [In English] Assembly establishment sent as its representatives abroad and at home and continued to oversee the activities [No interpretation] [In English] ... as a result of the [indiscernible] in favour of independence at the B-and-H-wide referendum on this issue on 29th February, 1st March 1992.
